slides.title: The Brand Audience
slides.subtitle: "Everyone" is not an audience. It is the most expensive way to reach no one.

slides.title: A beautiful product and no traction
slides.lead: He told me his app was "for everyone with a smartphone." Those two facts were related. Then one day he changed one sentence.
slides.why: the chapter opens on exactly this shape — one product, and 'the day he decided his product was for freelance designers who bill hourly and lose money to scope creep' everything downstream changed

tracks.label: "for everyone with a smartphone"
notes: no message, no channel to choose

tracks.label: "for freelance designers who lose money to scope creep"

slides.title: The instinct is not laziness. It looks like ambition.
slides.lead: If your product is good, why would you *voluntarily* exclude anyone?
bullets: Being useful to many people is not the same as being **for** a specific person. Those are different claims, and they activate different things in a buyer's mind.
"This is for you" is a signal that requires specificity to carry. "This is for everyone" carries no signal at all, because it requires no discrimination.
We are back in Spence territory: a signal is only as useful as the cost-structure that makes it informative. **"For everyone" is zero cost to say.**
It tells the listener nothing about whether the product understands their specific problem.

slides.title: Three ways an undefined audience defeats you
slides.lead: The empirical consequences are predictable, and they converge.
slides.why: chapter names exactly three consequences — 'dilutes the message … wastes budget … corrupts the product roadmap' — and the figure has all three converging on 'a brand that becomes illegible'

slides.title: Choosing an audience is choosing whom to disappoint
slides.lead: That refusal is not a limitation. It is what makes the brand legible.
bullets: You cannot have a principled basis for deciding whose request matters most until you have decided whose requests you are listening to.
The founder was probably *right* that his product would help any knowledge worker. Being right about that did him no good at all.
Specificity is the cost that makes the signal informative — the same mechanism, all the way down from Chapter 2.

slides.title: STP: the sequence is the point
slides.lead: Segmentation, Targeting, Positioning. Each step is built on the one before it — and no step can be skipped.
slides.why: chapter states 'the sequence matters' and 'Positioning is built on top of targeting'; whether your own market clears each stage is a thing only your work can answer

gates.label: Segmentation
gates.rule: divide into groups with genuinely different needs

gates.label: Positioning
gates.rule: a specific place in the target's mind

slides.title: Five ways to cut the same population
slides.lead: Each basis gives you a different cut through one market. They are not equally good.
slides.why: chapter enumerates five named bases, each with its own listed sub-criteria — 'demographic (age, income, occupation), geographic (region, urban/rural density), behavioral …' — a genuine two-level taxonomy

children.label: what they are trying to accomplish
a shared need, not a shared age
this is what defines a segment

slides.title: "Women 25–34" is a description, not a segment
slides.lead: Stopping at demographics is where most audience work dies.
bullets: The women in that description want dozens of different things — different jobs, different anxieties, different purchasing criteria.
What makes a group a **segment** is a shared *need*, not a shared demographic.
Two people with nothing demographically in common can belong to the same segment if they are trying to solve the same problem.
STP was formalized when marketing data was largely demographic and survey-based. The tools available shaped the bases. Behavioral data changed what is tractable.

slides.title: A strategic bet with two inputs
slides.lead: Fit: does the segment's need connect to what you actually do well? Winnability: can you reach them, and can you be meaningfully better than what they use now?
slides.why: chapter names both disqualifying cases outright — 'a segment that is a perfect fit but unreachable is not a target. A reachable segment where you offer nothing distinctive is not a target either'

slides.title: There is no mental slot for "everything"
slides.lead: Positioning — which Chapter 6 develops fully — is claiming a specific place in the target's mind: what you are, who you are for, and why you over the alternatives.
bullets: Positioning is built on top of targeting. It cannot be done first, and it cannot be done for everyone.
This is why the sequence in STP is not bureaucratic ordering. Skip a step and the next one has nothing to stand on.
Needs-based segmentation became tractable as behavioral data — purchase history, clickstream, usage logs — became available. **JTBD is what happens when you take it seriously all the way down.**

slides.title: Customers do not buy products. They hire them.
slides.lead: Clayton Christensen's reframing, from *Competing Against Luck*, starts from an uncomfortable observation.
bullets: The question stops being "who is this person" and becomes "what job is this person hiring this thing to do?"
Not what they *get* — that is the feature. What does having your work **accomplish** for them, in the context of the moment they turn to you?
"I need to look competent in front of a nontechnical executive in forty-eight hours" is specific enough to design for.
"Software engineers" is not.

slides.title: The method, in four moves
slides.lead: A fast-food chain hired a research firm to increase milkshake sales. The usual segmentation found nothing actionable — so the team changed the question.
slides.why: chapter narrates the study as ordered stages with stated outcomes: demographic and psychographic segmentation 'found nothing actionable', then direct observation, then the job, then the design changes

gates.label: Name the job
gates.rule: tolerable commute, full until lunch, no mess

gates.label: Name the real competitor
gates.rule: a banana, a granola bar, a bagel

output.label: thicker · wider straw · faster to dispense

slides.section: why the job is the segment
slides.title: A job cuts across demographics. Demographics cannot cut across themselves.
slides.lead: A 22-year-old graduate student and a 55-year-old executive may hire the same brand for the same job.
bullets: That shared job **is** the real segment.
If you had segmented by demographics, you would have separated them.
The shared job unites them in a way that actually predicts purchase and retention. The age bracket predicts nothing.
The real competitor is never the category. It is everything else that could do the job.

slides.title: The strongest brands resolve a tension, not a task
slides.lead: Douglas Holt, *How Brands Become Icons*: a contradiction or anxiety in the broader culture that a significant group feels and nobody is addressing.
bullets: Nike in its early mass-market phase was not selling shoes to athletes. It spoke to an anxiety about personal achievement in an era of corporate downsizing. **"Just Do It" was not a product promise.** It was a resolution: effort is still meaningful, and here is the uniform for it.
Dove's "Real Beauty" ran the same structure. The soap had not changed. The brand took a position in a conversation no major personal-care brand had entered.
The cultural tension *was* the unserved segment.
So ask one more question after you have the job: what tension does this group live with that no brand in your space is currently resolving?

slides.title: From a description to something magnetic
slides.lead: My brand: helping working engineers decide whether to move into management. Watch the audience definition sharpen, one rung at a time.
slides.why: chapter climbs this exact ladder in the worked example — the demographic 'is where most people stop', then the need, then 'the JTBD framing sharpens it further', then the cultural tension, which is 'dramatically more magnetic'

rungs.note: software engineers, mid-sized tech, ages 28–40 — where most people stop

rungs.note: told I should manage · cannot find honest information about what the transition costs

rungs.note: decide under uncertainty without paying the full cost of learning through failure

slides.title: The plausible invention feels exactly like knowledge
slides.lead: A persona is a research artifact: a concrete portrait grounded in evidence. The failure mode — especially with AI-assisted work — is the vivid portrait with no referent in reality.
bullets: It has a name, a job title, a commute, a weekend hobby, a fear. It is **specific enough to design for**, which is precisely the problem.
You will design for a person who may not exist, optimize for a problem they may not have, and ship into a gap that is not there.
What separates a real persona from an invention is what separated a separating signal from a pooling one: *verifiability*.
A real persona has at least one behavioral claim you can tie to evidence you could show someone — an interview quote, a support-ticket pattern, a forum thread in their own words.

slides.title: Every non-trivial claim earns a status tag
slides.lead: Confirmed: I have evidence. Needs evidence: I believe it, unverified. Inferred: I derived it from something I did confirm.
slides.why: chapter tags each worked-example claim by name — Jordan's fear 'confirmed' from three forum threads, Jordan's async preference 'needs evidence', Alex's Slack use 'inferred … not directly confirmed for this specific persona'

data.note: Mostly 'needs evidence' = a hypothesis, not a research artifact.

slides.title: AI drafts the persona. It cannot decide the persona is true.
slides.lead: This is the exact point where AI assistance is most useful and most dangerous.
slides.why: the chapter's own When-to-use / When-not-to-use lists name the boundary and its three refused crossings — committing to a target segment, accepting a persona as real, inventing market-size statistics

slides.title: Two things I cannot close
slides.lead: The honest limits of the two frameworks this chapter just sold you.
bullets: **JTBD assumes the job is stable enough to be discovered by observation.** If purchase is substantially driven by social contagion — buying because others buy, with no stable underlying job — then the segmentation it enables may be post-hoc rationalization. The contagion evidence is real. I cannot fully reconcile it.
**The cultural lens works when it works.** Nike and Dove hit genuine moments. Plenty of brands ran the same methodology and produced campaigns that read as opportunistic.

The difference seems to involve whether the brand's behavior over time is consistent with the position, or whether the campaign is the first time it showed up in that conversation. I cannot reduce that to a clean principle.

slides.section: what this deck does not tell you
slides.title: Every grey slot is a thing you have to go and find out
slides.lead: The chapter states no market sizes, no conversion rates, no segment counts. So this deck states none.
bullets: Whether *your* candidate segment clears fit and winnability — **TO RUN**.
How many of your persona claims are confirmed versus hypothesis — **TO RUN**, and the only way to fill it is contact with real humans.
Inventing market-size or behavior statistics is the one failure this whole chapter is built to prevent. A number you cannot show someone is worse than a blank.

slides.title: Name the segment. Then name whom you are willing to disappoint.
slides.lead: Draft three candidate segments by need or job — none of which could be summarized as "people who like [adjective] things." Pick one. Write two personas, tag every claim, and go find the evidence for one of them this week.
